doc.title: Jane Jarvis interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995

title: Her piano style and accompanying horns
summary: Rowe compares her playing to Brubeck; she explains how she accompanies different horns differently depending on register and phrasing.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Yeah. Neat. When I listen to you play, I’m thinking, first I heard your recording, before I heard you live, I felt like I was being taken back, almost to a ballroom type of style, and then said oh, it’s not quite that pretty. You’ve really got some nice rhythmic things happening there and some really muscular type playing. And last night I’m listening to you and I’m thinking, it sounds like Dave Brubeck took lessons from you or something.
Oh that’s so wonderful to hear. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
Yeah. I mean you tend to like to play two-handed style sometimes, and it really punches—

Yeah, I’m so respectful of harmony. But each, you see each musician, if you’re accompanying a horn instrument for example, you must play differently underneath them. You find what you think sounds good, but it won’t sound that good on every song. It’s something that applies right that given moment in time, and no other. But you don’t play the same thing beneath a trombone that you do under a tenor. I mean it depends what register they’re using or whether they’re playing legato or whether they’re playing in a breathy fashion. So this is what you call instant assessment of what you’re doing.
